title: Absolute usage sanity checker for stream slices and mid-stream handoffs
creator: Sofia Rivera
description:
Problem: We have subtle mismatches between the end-to-end billed token totals and what clients expect for long-lived streaming sessions. Root causes seen in production include: 1) resuming streams with overlapping prefixes, 2) mid-stream model handoffs that change tokenizer/quantization behavior, 3) compressed or chunked frames where client-side length encoding differs from server tokenization, and 4) partial-finalization when sessions abort mid-chunk. These lead to overcharges, user complaints, and flaky quota enforcement.

Goal: Implement a deterministic, end-to-end "sanity checker" validation harness and lightweight production probes that can assert, for a given session trace, that the billed token totals are equal to the canonical tokenization + finalization rules. The checker must run in CI, in a post-commit verifications job, and as an offline audit job that samples production traces to detect regressions.

Scope: This ticket covers the design and implementation of the checker, canonicalization rules for stream slices, CI integration, and a first audit pass over 7 days of sampled production session traces. Follow-up tickets will implement automated reconciliation/repairs and customer-facing billing adjustments if discrepancies are found.
acceptance_criteria: A deterministic canonicalizer function is defined and checked into runtime (single source of truth for token counting across streaming finalization semantics).
Unit tests cover resume-with-overlap, mid-stream-model-swap, compressed-frame, and abort-mid-chunk cases with golden token counts.
A CI job runs the checker against the runtime test harness and fails on any delta > 0 between billed tokens and canonical tokens.
An offline audit job runs against 7 days of sampled production streaming traces and produces a discrepancy report with session IDs and root-cause tags.
Dashboard card created in console-ops showing daily discrepancy rate, top session patterns, and estimated customer impact dollars.
steps: Design canonicalization rules and document with examples (contributor: Marco Li).
Implement canonicalizer in runtime codebase as an independent module with deterministic tokenizer invocation.
Extend session tracing to emit canonicalization checkpoints (start-offset, resume-offset, final-offset) in trace events.
Build checker harness that replays trace fragments through the canonicalizer and compares to persisted billed totals.
Add CI job to run harness on PRs touching metering/streaming code paths.
Run offline audit over sampled traces and triage top 50 discrepant sessions.
Create dashboard and an alert if daily discrepancy rate > 0.1% or if any single customer sees > $50 discrepancy.
design_decisions: Use server-side canonical tokenizer for checks rather than client-reported lengths to avoid client variance.
Checkpoint markers will be minimal and only include offsets and hash of last stable chunk to limit PII leakage in traces.
Checker will be read-only and non-intrusive; it will not alter billing records. Any repair flow will be a separate ticket.
Sampling will be stratified across model families, session lengths, and inbound regions to increase signal for rare cases.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Runtime canonicalizer changes could diverge from production billing path and create false positives. Mitigation: keep canonicalizer implementation small and run dual-mode against current billing function for two weeks before CI enforcement.
Risk: Tracing sensitive content. Mitigation: only store offsets and chunk hashes; do not persist raw prompt/completions to audit tables. Use KMS-protected buckets for ephemeral traces.
Risk: High-volume audit jobs add load. Mitigation: run offline on pre-aggregated trace exports and limit to a 1% sample initially.
